translation:
...hot and dry. And by these signs one shall recognize him: he has a pale complexion, like ashes, and this means that the fluid (moisture) has been consumed in him by the heat. He drinks more than he needs. As to his body, he is lean and yet has much flesh; his face is thin and gaunt, and he is quick to anger, though his anger passes quickly. He is swift in his deeds and is bold and quick in all his undertakings; he has no restraint in his speech, and he does not forget (grudges). He has a hard heart, yet he is generous, and does not consider to whom he gives. His worth lies in his heart, and his bones are coarse, as are his veins. He is quick and brisk and not sluggish. He desires women eagerly, but cannot manage much [with them]. Thus one may recognize the choleric type.

The phlegmatic resembles water and winter, for he is cold and moist, and these are his signs: he is pale/white in complexion, corpulent, and suffers from sluggish limbs, because he has no heat in him. He is soft and willingly obedient; he is fearful and not bold, and is not cheerful. He eats much and drinks little, and is slow in his affairs; he has soft hair and does not desire many women, yet he can manage much [with them], because he is cold — and naturally all women are cold and moist. And therefore a wise physician who [treats] wounds...

[The physician] wishing to treat must be careful that he recognize the nature and complexion of the person, that he know whether the person has a clear [pure] or soft, growing body, as children and some women do, and [whether he has] a moist temperament; to such clear and moist flesh belongs a drying medicine, because the body is moist. He should also observe whether the person has a dry body and flesh, as a person around forty years of age does, and also those who labor much and travel much are naturally dry in body; to such a one he must give a very drying medicine. And sometimes it happens that the moist nature becomes dry, and the dry becomes moist; in this matter the physician must be very careful that he go from one medicine to another according to how he observes the person, so that he does not make the moist dry, nor the dry moist, nor the hot cold, nor the cold hot. Also some members of a person are of a much drier nature than others, such as the bones [?] and the [artery/vessel?], and therefore they need a stronger drying medicine than the others. [The] ... is much different in the person than [the rest].

translation: That they have filled the empty places where there is neither flesh, vein, nor gut, and this is called according to the rule of the trade [term uncertain]. And therefore every physician should be diligent when he wishes to produce granulation (proud flesh) and fresh flesh in the wound, so that he prepares the medicine according to the nature and complexion of the person, and especially in wounds that do not readily wish to heal. You should note that there are many kinds of wounds that befall people, such as stabbed, cut, struck, shot, or from falling. And in all these and other wounds a physician should be careful: some wounds are to be sewn, and the seam should be neat, and he should be skillful and quick about it; and some wounds are not to be sewn — those he should leave alone according to his art. Also note that some wounds are mortal, some are harmful but long-lasting (curable over time), and some are harmful but not long-lasting. The mortal wounds are such as when the heart is wounded, and the stomach, and the bladder, and the liver, and other internal organs of the person; and whoever is wounded in the head such that the brain comes out — in all such wounds God the Lord is the best physician. Yet Master Hugo has healed many in whom a great part of the brain had come out, and remarkably...

translation:
[AI TRANSCRIPTION, LOW CONFIDENCE -- NEEDS SCHOLARLY REVIEW: Dense Gothic cursive with many abbreviations and archaic medical terminology makes exact word-for-word transcription highly uncertain despite a generally coherent reading of the content.]
When the belly is wounded in such a way that it swells or bulges and festers, or that the fire [fever] takes hold of it — that is death.

The stab-wounds and lame (paralyzing) wounds are all wounds where there is not much flesh and many sinews; and these are the wounds of the hands and the bones (limbs), and of the running (tendons) and of the joints, and of the sinews and of the hair-wash [hamstring?], which are called 'lacerti,' and four fingers above the knee and four fingers below, and near the ankle. If the bones are struck off or broken there, that is all stab-like and lame, and sometimes deadly.

When such a wound befalls a person, he readily falls into unrest so that he cannot sleep, and he cramps up, with great pain; and also the cramp comes to the wound, above all wounds upon a person and travels [spreads]. It is useful and good for the doctor to give the person a stool [purgative/laxative? or a specific remedy] made for this, so that the bad vapors/humors do not settle at the wound and corrupt it further.

And for falling wounds that recur to a person, the doctor should bring forth and prepare an emetic and a purgative from the stomach, from above.

And if it happens that a great flow [of blood] from a bone-wound occurs, then heal only the wound and let the bone alone; otherwise, if you wish to heal the bone but not the wound, then the person may get spasm — that is, cramp [convulsion].

translation:
How much blood there be, whether much or little, and all great wounds that need [treatment].

The harmful wounds on limbs — that is, all fresh wounds — require only a strong, pain-relieving [remedy] together with a common medicine that belongs to it; and all fresh wounds require more of a dry medicine, while the small ones never [need it]. It is reported that all wounds require dry medicine, except only the wounds of the belly, which cannot tolerate it. In all deep, straight, long or short wounds you should be diligent to fit the lips of the wound well together; and if they need stitching, then stitch them. And the deep ones you should heal from the bottom up, so that nothing unclean or full of pus remains within, unhealed. Also note that all wounds which appear healed but still have matter (pus) inside must be cut open again, so that the pus and the impurity flow out. How you should cut — that is taught by the size of the wound and its nature. You should know that there is no better medicine for all wounds than good wine. Warm wine draws out the pus very quickly, as Hippocrates says, for wine renews and strengthens nature; and nature makes good flesh in man, and good flesh produces good blood, for there is no greater source in all wound medicine than this.

translation: [When] nature is robbed of its blood and the doctor cannot bring it back again, it is therefore necessary that the doctor come to the aid of the wounded man with good food, that is natural for him, and with good wine, so that nature may return and the sick person may again gain good, fresh, natural flesh and blood. And also above all things the wounded man should guard himself against unchastity and against shame with women, for shame brings desire, and desire brings deeds [works of the flesh]. You should also note that when nature does not have good food and good drink to make good flesh and fresh blood, then you can do nothing—neither with the clamp [splint] nor with the great wounds—by way of work or effect. Therefore a wise doctor should know the diet needed by the wounded patient, and feed him accordingly so that he may gain fresh, new, raw flesh and blood. And he should give him the food in moderation, according to the time of day. He should also take care that he does not give the patient food mixed with food that is not useful to him, so that nature is not hindered and the doctor's work is not prolonged. The foods that make good blood for him are good hens, capons, [and] young chickens.

translation: Good meat: young swan meat, partridge, pheasant, lamb, wild fowl, and good soup made from old hens, and good fresh eggs beaten into water and cooked therein — such and other good foods. A drink should be good old white wine. And moreover, for everyone whose wound is severe, the food and regimen should be adapted according to his nature; that is, for him the harmful remedies [should be avoided], and especially in the case of women. The species [remedies/simples] for wounds that are cold and hot, and that dry out the [wound near the] nose, are: henbane seed, mandrake, and celery/parsley. Of these every physician should beware, for although it is true that they dry the wounds very much, they nevertheless cool the wounds excessively. Also beware of resin — that is, of pine-pitch and black pitch — for these are excessively hot; you should not place them on a fresh wound unless you have first mixed them with a cooling remedy. Also note: if the air is cold, then give a hot remedy; but if it is hot, then give a cold remedy. Also note the remedies that generate flesh and produce it, as Galen says: that is, frankincense, barley flour and bean [flour], vetch, iris, mugwort plant, opopanax, and [thuria?] — and these are, some more drying, some less; some have a simple power, some a compounded power, for [continues]...

translation:

In all limbs from the head down to the feet, this is very helpful for the wounds: that you take sweet pomegranate ('granati dulcs') and soften it, and set it upon the wound with wine and water. You should also observe the appearance of the discharge: if you see with the ointment (?) that the wound becomes red and swollen, then help it with cold remedy and with ointment 'albo', that is, with white salve. But if you see that the wound becomes soft from ointment 'albo', then help it with ointment 'nigro', that is, with black salve. If the flesh in the wound becomes mortified from the blow, one should cut away that mortified flesh, [which is] rotten and festers with matter, and thus the wound is cleaned out well inside; when it festers, then afterward make a good flesh-poultice (fish-flesh?). You should also not lay dry remedy into the wound. Whichever wound you wish to make fester further, do not lay dry remedy into it, for the festering comes from moisture and heat. Every wound should be kept dry — except those which should not be [dried], namely the limbs at which the swelling (Drüse) is called; those one must treat with heat and moisture.

translation: ...and wound plasters. If the flesh of the wound is moist, that being the natural (proud) flesh, one should give it a dry medicine and protect it from water, and wash it with wine or with good vinegar. What flesh is hot, you should make cold, and what is cold, you should make hot — this you can recognize by the color of the flesh, and also by what the patient can endure, and also by whether the medicine applied to the wound is hot or cold. Take terebinth and common oil and barley meal and boil these together. First you should wash all wounds with warm wine, and then make a compress with a cloth to dry the wound.

Surgical Unguentum Apostolicum

Take ship's pitch (pix navalis), one pound of pitch; also ħ galbanum, sarapinum, armoniacum, opoponax, an equal weight; wax, weight II. Make these into a gum by grinding them as much as possible; lay them in vinegar and let them dissolve there in a copper pan over the fire — the galbanum and armoniacum and sarapinum and opoponax and ship's pitch — and let them melt together for a while; then pour it into cold water, and if it sets like tallow, then it is good. Afterward, take powdered Greek pitch and mastic and olibanum (frankincense), equal weights, and add these to it and stir it well together with the rest. This changes the wound's yellowish scar/wound-crust — it is good for this. Afterward take it off the fire, and add an equal weight of terebinth to it, and stir it well through the others. Caput [Head]: This is when the head is injured in such a way that a part of the skull is struck off but not entirely severed, and this same piece hangs down still attached by the skin. Then one should cut the skin in two down to the broken-off bone, and should thereafter loosen that same piece of bone from the skin and throw it away. Afterward fold the skin back up again, lift it from above, and stitch it on both sides very quickly and firmly with a silk needle, and in the middle, where you have cut it open, leave it open so that you may be able to heal the resulting wound well. You should also note that if much skin hangs down, you should cut all of it away together and discard it, for otherwise good scarring (healing) could not occur.

This is a healing (treatment) for wounds. But if it is torn to the bone and hangs down with the skin, then stitch it up and proceed in all things as written above; and when you have stitched the wound, lay the red powder upon it, made as follows. How to make the red powder:
Take greater comfrey (consolida maior) one drachm, bole (bolus) one drachm, dried peppercorns three drachms, mastic-gum an equal amount, ceruse (white lead) an equal amount, [and] two drachms of dragon's blood — grind all these to powder and keep it. This powder stops the blood and heals the flesh at the seam after stitching, and forms good skin over the wound. And when you have stitched the wound and applied the powder upon it, then lay at the end of the wound a plantain leaf or a compress, and afterward a poultice-cloth over that, so that the matter (pus) that flows out from the place of the wound is drawn off. And apply the powder twice each day upon the wound, and do this each day until you see the flesh grow and heal; then draw the threads out of the stitched wound, and afterward heal it with a plaster as written above. And in the seam of the wound that has been made by the physician (surgeon), lay a dry cloth on it, and so heal it as before. You should know that one leaves the threads at the stitching of a wound on the head in the wound for eight days, and otherwise [differently for other places].

Where a suture (stitching of a wound) occurs on the body, only after five or six days, as Hugo says: the powder of both consolida (comfrey) and frankincense with dragon's blood, or good burnt salt applied fresh to the stitched wound, removes the bad flesh and makes good flesh grow. If the head is wounded by a blow so that the skull is bent inward and the bone is cracked, so that the marrow (or brain) is affected — the sick person walks around as if in a dream, with enmity/confusion, and the sleep is disturbed and he vomits water and wants to defend himself — then one should cut it open and proceed as before. Hugo says that Apostolicon or Diatessaron mixed together help the skull [heal] where the wound-bed remains open a while, as long as it is kept clean. Galienus says the same, that in all skull-penetrating wounds of the head, however the wound occurs, one should [treat it] so that the middle bone is removed, unless it is too soft and does not go all the way through. When you see the pia mater (brain membrane), lift it out, and when you stitch the wound, first strew powdered frankincense on the wound, and afterward stitch it. If it happens that the throat/neck is wounded, whether with a sword or with a knife, then the physician should first examine the wound very well and gently probe it with his hands, to see whether there is anything within the wound that should be removed from it, such as splinters, wood, or some other foreign matter. If the flow of blood hinders (proper closure), then let him stitch part of the wound and leave part of it open; and when the bleeding has stopped, he should then remove from the wound whatever remains inside it that is done/decayed, and stitch it up well, yet so that it remains open on both sides for the sake of the pus (drainage). But if the cartilage (windpipe) or the artery in the neck is wounded, so that the cartilage/windpipe protrudes visibly from the wound, and breath comes out warm with a growth (swelling) that is very close at the edges, then one should cauterize it a little with a glowing iron, and afterward stitch the wound and proceed as written above.

And note that all veins that are wounded should first be cauterized with a hot iron, and afterward sutured, and then powder placed upon them, and afterward a compress with white or warm wine. And note: if the wound pains when you suture it, that means it is festering; and afterward suture it, and thus it will heal. Juice of burdock (sucus bardanae) is very good when applied, for it draws out the redness or the veins if one smears it there, and it helps the constricted (blocked) veins. If the neck-vein is often wounded but not completely severed, the physician must be skillful and should first suture it above and below near the arteries of the wound, so that he does not prick or catch anything with the needle; rather he should pass the thread and needle around the vein and bind it tightly so that it does not bleed. And if it is that you [seek] good healing power for life, then draw it out at once, and it takes about six days. Rogerius says: if the measuring-wound and the face is shot as well near the eyes, and into the nostrils, and into the cheek, and the arrow-shaft remains fixed there, though it is that the arrow is very difficult to extract, yet the physician shall, according to his own judgment, work and consider how he may win [free] the arrow with the shaft. He shall, next to the shaft, leave a small wick (wound-dressing) made of cloth or of tow in the wound, and let it lie in the wound folded over; thereafter, before the shaft, [use] the length as needed, [and] draw carefully; he brings it out, gives thanks. There it is to be feared, when one wishes to draw out the arrow, that very easily the iron may remain in the stomach or in the belly, and if the arrow(head) remains within, one must be very much on guard, for it is greatly to be feared that the person may die of it. Then the physician should make a plaster of clay [loam], and see to it that he applies power, and lay the plaster upon the place where one now feels the point of the arrow, and upon the plaster lay the thumb around it, and press the arrow very swiftly so that it may be drawn back out from there. Then the physician should press the surrounding flesh together very firmly with the left hand near the shaft, and with the right hand he should draw out the shaft very gently and with all diligence, so that the iron remains properly in the stomach or the belly. And if the physician perceives that in drawing the shaft he feels the iron [move], he should push the shaft back in so that the iron [pierces properly], and whoever has his thumb against the point of the arrow upon the skin should press very firmly, so that the arrowhead adheres well to the shaft. And while the assistant presses firmly with the thumb, the physician should also press with his left hand the surrounding flesh near the wound of the shaft, and meanwhile he should move the shaft and gradually draw it out further and further.

[In this text, Rogerius (the medieval surgical authority Roger of Salerno) describes the healing of a certain condition over a number of days, with treatment applied on specified days as before.]

I apply the first bandage; on the third day I lift it off and bandage again as before, and afterward, after the third day, on into the ninth day I make a plaster, namely "Stratorium Rogerii." Take the above-mentioned powder and mix it very well with the white of one egg, and then take a long piece of flax, soak it well in this mixture, and lay it flat around the rupture/wound, and bandage it with a bandage as before, and let it remain so until the wound is well healed.

And if it swells, then wash the area with mallow and bear's-breech [acanthus] and let the threads [sutures?] stay loose, and when you see that the rupture is standing well and without any hindrance, then make the "Spadadarpfium Rogerii." Take powder of mastic, sumac, and burnt pearl [or similar ingredients], and lay this upon it, together with wax and heated tallow, and let this cook together on the fire with another [ingredient], and afterward spread it on a cloth and bind it onto the rupture, so that it is this way: the member will afterward grow strong.

Then anoint the rupture with oil of althea (marshmallow) or with oil of marjoram, and lay a compress upon it, and bind it well, and if the member is still soft and weak, do it again in the same way.

The arm, from the elbow down to the hand, is made of two bones, so that one, the lower one, is near the little finger — that is the smaller one — but the one near the thumb is large and often breaks; that smaller bone is more harmful [to break] than the larger one, and the larger one often breaks too, and is likewise harmful; and often both break together. The breaking of the toes and their dislocation is in all respects the same as with the fingers of the hand. Now I have taught concerning the fracture of the bones of all limbs and concerning their joints and so forth. Now I will teach concerning the dislocation of all limbs, how a physician should proceed when one limb separates from another. Dislocatio is called the 'going-out' or dislocation of the limbs — when it happens that a limb goes out of joint, the physician must hurry so that he sets it back before it swells. For if the physician does not hurry and it takes too long, the dislocated limb swells; and when the limb has swollen, you should not move it nor shake it nor try to set it back in, for from this often comes lameness and also much delay/damage. And when the swelling is hot and red, then apply cupping (set the cupping-glass) on it, and thereafter [continue as follows]...

translation: Pain in the head, and the person might easily die from it; therefore to avoid all this, a physician should hasten, and when he wants to set the jaw, the assistant should hold the head, and the physician should put his thumb into the mouth and move the bone back and forth on both sides, and then set it evenly straight, so much that the lower teeth align evenly with the upper ones. After that, put the bone back into its place, or help it, as this is called the treatment. If the person has a swelling, let him go to a bath, for when the joining comes hard upon it, and in the bath let the swelling be softened with warm water and with oil — this process of softening is called "waiken" — until the swelling becomes soft. After that, fit him: let him sit upright with his back straight, and let the assistant hold the head between the ears and also grasp the ends of the jawbone. Then the master should put his thumb into the mouth and move the jaw back and forth, and stretch it evenly so that the lower teeth align with the upper ones. And if this does not help, then the doctor should take two strong men - one to hold the arm from behind and another before the arm - and let them stretch very firmly. A hand stretches thus from the fingers up to the joint of the arm, and is called the hand. The hand becomes easily dislocated, and becomes very difficult to set back into its place. Now, it is so that the leg becomes

happens backward, so that

in place, and the head of the bone is bent
to one side — thus you may recognize it.

Concerning the break of the bone, therefore the doctor should be careful that he brings the bone back together before the swelling and moisture set in, which would cause the bone to rot and be entirely ruined. Therefore he should have the patient's bone stretched out properly, and he should move it back and forth with both hands and make the place even from which it came out, and bring it back into its place. After that, bind it and set it as taught before. But when it is dislocated out of the joint, then the doctor should have the patient kneel, and a strong man should hold the patient from above, and the doctor should take the head of the bone and fit it back with his hands into its place, from which it came. After that, bind it as before.

When it happens that the knee becomes dislocated, the patient should sit on a stool close to the ground, and his feet should be lifted up a little. After that, a strong man should take his knee below and above and stretch it; then the master should fit it back into its proper place. There is no danger in this—you may bone-set, salve, and bind the knee, and the patient should move and guide the knee to bend.

translation:
Let the mixture boil, then strain it
through a cloth, and that which has been strained should again
be put into a kettle or pan, and add to it
one lot of wax in summer and in
winter five lots, and let the wax melt.
Then make a powder of olibanum (frankincense) and
mastic and verdigris, each one lot,
and put the powders into the kettle and mix
them well together; and before you put in the
verdigris, you should first test the salve
to see whether it will hold together. Then
put in the verdigris and stir it
well together, and if it is not
green enough, add more verdigris
to it. Afterward take it off the fire
and add to it one lot of liver-colored aloe, made
into a powder, and let it dissolve in the oil, and
so you will have the green ointment (unguentum viride); this ointment
is good for all wounds — it produces fresh
flesh and draws out the impurities. For
running, troublesome wounds (ulcers), apply this salve.

Take liver-colored aloe, vitriol,
and olibanum in equal parts, and make them into powder.
Then take flour and fine turpentine (?)
in equal measure, and take the juice from it, and
then pour in the liquid a little
at the powder and mix it together with
the rest, and afterward pour in oil and
mix it, and from that pour off the remainder as before.

Take three lot of unslaked lime and set that to boil, cut up, in water; and three lot of alum (pigment/mineral form) and lay it in the lime, and let it thus boil so long that when you dip a feather into it and immediately draw it out, the lye has consumed the feather's plume — then it is [strong/ready] enough. After that, take it off the fire, and when you have plucked out the hair with the stalk/root, and smear the red [substance] onto the skin, then anoint the head again and proceed as before, and do this until the skin becomes white. And if all this does not help, then make this salve: Take of [strafagria?] seed one lot, and white hellebore one lot, and verdigris pigment, vitriol, alum, of each one lot, and galbanum one lot; grind all these to powder, and pound with [six?] lot of expressed oil, and mix the powder with it. After that take flamula (buttercup) and wormwood and centaury and smoke-wort (fumitory) and spurge (tithymalus) and saltpeter, each a handful; press these and extract the juice therefrom, and put the juice into the oil, and let it boil together again. Afterward take six lot of pitch and add that too, and let it boil together with the rest, and with this ointment anoint the head. If it is that the scabby crust (grind) is rough/scaly, then add quicksilver to the ointment, mixed with dead spittle (i.e., saliva that has been killed/neutralized). If it is that the scab is not old, so that it is only a year old, then it heals...

...and let the hair not smoke out [i.e. let it stay in]. Take agrimony (agrotam agrestis) and dandelion herb (herbe stauren) and fennel and mugwort (artronole), each a handful, and pound them well in oil, and let the oil stand for a day and a night. And afterward rub this together well and anoint the head with it: it heals the scabs and the scald, and afterward put the powder made above onto it. Take sage and white southernwood, of each two lot [an ounce measure], and make this into a powder, and apply it as long as the head swells. Item: take my soot and grease and mix them together, and when you have pulled out the hair, spread the powder on it and bind it before [applying] to the head with vinegar, and anoint it also with honey and afterward with the powder. Item: take my mouse and put it in a fresh [state/skin] and roast it on the fire, and let it roast thus, and afterward break it open, and whatever fat runs out from it, anoint the scald with that. Item: also you shall know that: my wormwood and southernwood and betony and fennel seed and boil them in water. Item: burnt alum, one lot, and unslaked lime, three lot, mix these with vinegar. Item, a good salve: take litharge, three lot, and make it into powder, and then add a little of it [oil?] and mix it, and afterward a little vinegar, and thus make it until it becomes a salve, and it will [heal].

translation:
This is how you make [a remedy] for the sore: take the juice of elder-wort and asphodel root, and staphisagria. This is also a good powder: take old bran and burn it to powder, and also take chickpeas, make them into powder, and mix these two together.

This is a good plaster for scabs: oil and good resin, and the powder of staphisagria and litharge mixed together, and from another preparation you make a plaster. Also, [take] the root of sharp dock and the root of scabious, let them boil well in oil, then strain it, and add to that oil the powder of litharge and staphisagria, and let these boil together until [it is done]. Also, my plaster: [use] pure juice and fat of an unseasoned lard and mix this together — it is good for all kinds of scab/mange.

Also, the juice of sharp dock, boiled and [applied] warm, and washed on the head, increases the hair. Of many salves and powders called "of the Apostles" [apostolorum]:

In Vienna and [elsewhere], scholars came together and learned to make many kinds of salves and powders, and for medicine he teaches how to make a good old salve called the "Ointment of the Apostles." Take Greek pitch and wax and resin and ammoniac gum, of each four lot; and opopanax and flower of bronze (verdigris), four lot; and galbanum and white frankincense and bdellium, of each one lot; and olibanum and myrrh, of each one lot; and litharge, one lot — these gums you shall boil in one [vessel].

A strong quarter-measure of vinegar until it becomes warm. Then add the pitch and the resin (hartz), and the wax together, and take a bit of olive oil and add that too, and let it melt together gently, and do not stir it through another vessel so that it does not burn, and let it cool. The salve will then all be uniform. It heals fistulas and all wounds and all swellings, and cleanses unclean flesh and rotten flesh. Thus you have made the ointment of the apostles.

Ointment of the Apostles

A salve called "apostolicam" — make it thus: take black pitch and Greek pitch, of each a half-ounce, and take galbanum and serapinum and ammoniacum and opoponax, of each one lot, and six lots of wax, and a half-ounce of vinegar, and let all of this simmer together a little. Afterward take mastic and frankincense, well powdered, and bladder-pitch and turpentine, of each one lot, and let that melt together with the rest. Afterward strain it through a cloth, then into cold water, and dip it — not through the cloth — then take it off the top from the water, and rub your hands with oil and hold it by the fire until it becomes soft.

Powder of sarcocolla, 5 lot, and add also
thereto, and mix this with another, and
to it add some collyrium (eye-salve) and also
hepatic aloes, 5 lot, and make it into powder,
and moisten it with a little oil, very well,

with a piece of wood very thoroughly with another,
afterward press it out through a cloth,
and keep this, and when the need arises,
spread this salve out, and apply it to the eye with
a feather, gently, as the master instructs.

If anyone [suffers] from a film over the eyes,
[where] the eye becomes clouded and the film
spreads so that it covers vision, here is help: take
clove-oil and galangal, ginger, likewise
calamine stone that has been newly fired,
washed and prepared, often as described, by the quintal [measure];
crush the calamine first very finely,
then crush also the other ingredients and make
them into powder, and mix all of this together
with another substance; then take some prepared
material and add it, and make it thick like
fine flour, and mix it not too much,
and apply this each day, stirred, into the eyes.

If it happens that a blister forms on the eye itself
and it becomes very sore, then one should keep
dust and debris from entering the eye at all, for
from such irritation the blood and the eye may
become damaged; therefore help it in this way: take
an egg and boil it until it becomes hard,
in vinegar; afterward peel it and apply that [to the eye].

Take three lots [measures] each of salt and water-pearls, finely ground, one lot,
and make all of this into a powder.
Mix this with pounded honey,
well prepared, and let it
simmer together, and keep it, and take of it every

strengthens the sight of the eyes and
also the eyes, and the excessive discharge

for the eyes: take castoreum and frankincense (olibanum)

the verdigris; grind it to a powder and lay
it upon a hot marble stone and
spread the powder out and stir it back

put it into water and grind it further and stir it well.

pearls to a fine powder and mix them,

well, and set it in the sun and let
it dry; after the third day, make it
into powder again and mix it once more with
rosewater, and set it out of the sun
in a dark place, and do this three times in
all over nine days; then keep it, for this is the best
powder for cleansing the eyes,
such as when an eye has been struck and
a bruise has formed, or blood lies
upon the eyes, or when the eye has become swollen.

Ointment against morphea (a skin disease)

For morphea, take tartar and [illegible], lead white, burnt orpiment, rock crystal, vitriol, soap, spatan, and ointment. Take litharge and white wax, common oil, weasel oil, and laurel oil, as well as cumin fat, pepper, mastic, and frankincense. translation:
Of the remaining [herbs], make a plaster with wool and
anoint and put it in and bind it over the
ear. ¶ Another: boil wax, and after-
ward fill the wax with oil from nuts
and with thyme powder, and melt the wax
well by the fire; afterward
press out the juice and put three drops
into the ear, and from the remaining matter make
another plaster as before. ¶ Another: take
wormwood juice and oil and mix it,
lay that into the wax and let it
simmer inside; afterward press the juice out,
and when it has cooled, lay the wax,
still warm, upon it. ¶ If there is a pressure
in the ears, take dust-strew and hempseed
and boil that with styrax balsam and
with honey, and make a plaster from it,
and bind that over the pressure, so it will
soften. ¶ Another: take rue and
white of an egg, roast it well,
press it through a cloth and press
the juice out, and lay that juice into the
wax, and let it simmer therein,
and put the juice into the ear while still warm,
and bind the wax over the ear. ¶ If
there be a worm in the ear, take
oil and the juice of wormwood and
chamomile, and mix that very well together
with another, and let it drip into the ear;
that kills the worm. Also myrrh juice
and such, dripped into the ear, helps.

translation:
It kills the worm, and if drunk, it kills the worm
in the belly. [mark] By another: take oil and
lay therein an unslaked lime, and let
the lime dissolve within it, and afterward
strain it through a cloth, and put the oil
into the ears; this kills the worm. If, however,
you have a worm elsewhere, as in
the teeth or elsewhere, then take hellebore
and rub it with vinegar, and mix
it with oil, and spread it upon the limb
where the worm is; it kills the worm. If,
however, something has fallen into the ear, then
fetch it out gently with soft, slender hairs, and
do not reach too far in, so that you
do not damage the membrane, and if you
cannot get it out, then entrust it to God
the Lord, who is a master above all masters.

translation:
A fistula is a wound or ulcer of long standing, a kind of hollow,
which, having a narrow orifice and a wide base, does not
receive healing but instead continually discharges matter.
A fistula sometimes arises from an internal cause, as from corrupt
humor; sometimes from an external cause, as from a
wound badly treated; sometimes from an abscess, as from
a growth badly treated. And if the fistula should be near
the flesh, it discharges something watery.
If indeed it arose from an injury, it will have become putrid, as
the washing of flesh would show. If, however, it should be an injury
to the nerves, it discharges putrefied matter, dark in color,
affecting nerves, veins, and arteries, burnt
as if by cauterization, and so produces a fistula that
takes hold throughout all the members of the body, as
Albucasis says. If a fistula should occur near the great
veins, or near the arteries, or near the nerves, or
near the muscles and the intestines, or near the bladder, or near
some rib, or near some vertebra of the spine,
or near some part of the body, as in
the foot or hand — and among these, those that occur
in the principal members and sinews are, almost all,
difficult to heal and do not readily receive
treatment, requiring food, exertion, and fire [cautery]
as remedy. And I myself say that I had a relative
who for a long time had a fistula in his forearm
and hand, and many bones came out, and by treatment
was, through the efforts of a certain Hugo, very well
cured. And I saw a certain girl who for seven
years had had a fistula and an injury of the foot, and
by my counsel she was treated and cured. And likewise
I knew of a certain man, whom I remember, who suffered a fistula
whose depth penetrated between two ribs.
label: fol. 70r

translation:
...I completely cured him, although he suffered from a fistula in the lacrimal area, without an incision or cautery, I healed the fistula and consolidated the ulcer.

Fistulas are both recent and ancient, as kinds of hollows already established, deeply set in the flesh, vehemently; and such are difficult to heal, but it is necessary to eradicate that entire deep-seatedness so that one cuts away from every side, whether with iron (instrument) or with cautery, or with sharp medicine. But Avicenna says that sharp medicine is harmful and disquieting, and so it is, especially in the vicinity of nerves and noble members. I, however, say that I applied sharp medicine in the lacrimal fistula and mortified the fistula with much pain. I applied for eight days [some remedy/mixture], with great care and caution, and so that it might by chance be possible that it should wait and corrode if there be any oily matter delaying its progress, and that it should expire, leaving behind the remainder of its dead flesh, and that it should putrefy and remain so for a long space of time, but still it may not yet be fully putrefied through, and whoever wishes to heal it must strip the fistula of the deceptive oily flesh, then fill it with desiccative medicines, and then leave it. This, according to Avicenna, I do not praise, and I say that what he says is not possible; rather I say that if this is done, it will cause an abscess and will prevent the passage of discharge up to the opening, so that the fistula will rot further and the treatment will fail unless it is eradicated throughout, together with all its sides, and you must examine [treat] its tortuous crookedness. For I myself once cured a certain man who had a fistula in the lacrimal area, and I labored [over it]...

translation:
On the application of mercury, I say that it has no value where quicksilver is used in place of arsenic, to which I believe one hair is corrupted, or perhaps there was a crust formed in the wounds, and I say that every physician should treat with sharp medicines and should do this with care and caution.

But in fistulas that are old, one should wash them with medicine that is strong, so that mild things and sea water and soap water are dispensed to them. With strong harsh medicines, when it is required, one makes a mallet with [various ingredients], and purified water from burnt lime and ammoniac salt — do not shrink from this — and such water as distinguishes [the condition], or white lime made from eggs and quicklime, and in sum, purified water from purified arsenic, ammoniac salt, and sulfur, and this is wonderful.

And sublimated arsenic, thus prepared, is wonderful; it is called a fistula, and it is called cancer, and it is called a deceitful, poisoned ulcer. For this purpose a plaster of arsenic is made, which I say cures tearful and wonderful fistulas.

A moderate preparation is made from certain roots up to [a point], with wax and antimony, [and other ingredients], the substance of vetch and verjuice, from which I have had experience. On this same day the stem of the plant, when applied to a fistula, fills and heals it, and the golden root as well, and I myself have had experience and freed someone from a fistula by this means.

For burning sores, child's urine is good, without reservation, given and mixed in a vessel, with the root of spurge-laurel ground up and powdered, and mixed with honey and made into food, by which means the fistula is healed through to its complete cure.

translation:
I have weighed the question whether in every case the material is simple or composite, since a simple matter requires a simple cure. It should also be noted from the beginning whether it is sanguine or choleric in nature. For one who discharges blood in this condition, the blood appears thicker and has a greater and stronger pulse, being more red and broad on the surface. Choleric matter, however, is more yellowish and raised, being thinner and less colored.

Treatment of the sanguine condition from the start should be phlebotomy, performed in moderation. If tolerable, a purgative should then be given; after this, apply cold compresses to repel [the matter] and prevent the site from forming pus. For swellings, let there be lettuce pulped together with poppy, formed into pills, to soothe; apply with a little water, with flour mixed in as needed.

If in that place there is a tendency toward hardening as in a gland or knot, for swellings a warm compress is indicated; soften gently with a cloth as usual.

If matter has coagulated, soak with warm water and a little salt; for this, prepare a salted poultice and apply a plaster of rose water and barley flour as customary.

For abscesses of the blood, let there be a plaster made from the juice of [a plant] with flour of fenugreek mixed in, so that it may resolve; take care it does not drip onto a growth, so as not to cause a carbuncle; and apply a plaster of flour and coriander.

In abscesses caused by phlegm, once evacuated, let there be abstinence from foods that generate phlegm; let there be repeated application of drying and resolving agents as needed.

Partly offered and my little remedy and plaster for curing, with ointment made of deer horn, egg, oil, and salt.

Scrofulas and glands are hard swellings and difficult, since they arise from glands and are hardened by phlegm, and this is scrofula, as I say. And I distinguish scrofula from gland, since scrofula is hard and bound tight, similar to a stone, while the gland is softer and yields to the touch. And concerning scrofula, there are some that burst and others that remain enclosed; the hot matter and the ones near the ear are called by that name, each according to its kind.

The pains are difficult to cure and the surgeon's finger is often needed. And scrofulas that occur in infants are lesser evils, and worse are those that occur in young people and in the root where the condition is lodged, along with the swellings and their surrounding glands.

The treatment regimen: it will be healed as is customary, dissolved with grease and vinegar, and let it drink mixed [remedies]. And as is commonly said, one should take for seven days pills made from the juice of garlic, agrimony, and cucumber until the aforesaid matter is entirely consumed so that nothing remains.

And give to drink this preparation against the scrofula: new bran, polypody, grape tendrils, dragées of squill and acorus root, with honey-water, dissolved stechados, and cooked scrofularia, taken all together with pepper, coriander, cumin — one ounce — this shall be the remedy.

Roots and herbs shall be infused in the house to soften; take first a portion for half [a measure], and this should be finely ground, soft, and administered as a suppository.

translation:
Let it boil a little further, and let the powder of worm-wood [or similar substance] be strewn in; then let it be given from a vial, that is, by hand; and let it not be lost, so that one degree of its virtue should endure. Let the watery part be drawn off, so that from the body afterward it may be brought through the serum, anointed, Mary [?] -- according to this let it be smeared and mixed, and placed into the wound. Let a plaster be made: take theriac, turnip [?], steeped in honey and vinegar, divided and applied gently, so that it may heal.

Likewise, concerning swellings or glands: first they must be opened and treated by hand. As for the upper part, in the wound, let it be cleansed all around, strewn and anointed, and brought to healing. And concerning other matters that may happen besides, it is said that all these things should be washed there, according to the custom appropriate to the wound.

But if there be excessive bleeding in the limbs, let it be bound with cloth tightly wrapped around, filled with a piece of linen cloth soaked, which itself is better; and let powder be applied -- see first that it be a simple powder, made according to the proper proportions, so that the wound may be properly treated and said to be clean.

Concerning which, we shall further say little more.

[Red heading:] Distillations
of waters, and first, the distillation of rose water.

Let rose water be made thus: take fresh rose leaves [or petals] and crush them, and macerate them beforehand; and let them be pulverized, then placed into a mortar, pounded, and set [in a vessel], and distilled. Likewise for another water, take pepper, mint, rue, parsley, alexanders, cedar [wood], oil, and calamus stone; mix all these together and place them as before; let it boil until it is reduced, and strain the water through a cloth for use through the year. And let it be strained well and sealed for nine days.

translation:
[The remedy] is given to drink each day
for a number of days, for those who suffer this sickness,
on an empty stomach, fasting for
seven hours, and this medicine is one
of the methods, among medicines for such illness.
Taken thus, drunk on an empty stomach, it stops
all palsy of weakened limbs and strengthens
the nerves above all medicines. / Also drunk
on an empty stomach it cures the stomach so that all
gout and palsy [are cured], even if the paralysis is not
mortal in the weakened limbs. / Also taken as smoke it greatly helps
a wound infected with poison, if it is washed
with the same. / Also drunk on an empty stomach for
[several] days it drives away all fevers, however
long-standing they may have been.

Water for the eyes:

Water for the eyes is made thus: take agrimony,
rue, savory with apples and
mix with celandine and sugar and the stone
of the pomegranate, grind these and place in an alembic
for gentle distillation over the fire. This water, when first
applied, relieves eye pain however severe it turns out
to be, which cannot be cured by any other medicine, whoever
treats it with this remedy. / Also, drunk on an empty
stomach it expels all poison; drunk,
it protects the stomach from all evil
humors. / Also drunk it helps all dropsy
when cold water is used, and on the third day
it extinguishes the veins' fever, for example with hemp-tow
and dill placed as a poultice; this medicine
has great power against fire [fever].

This page contains a Latin recipe describing the preparation and virtues of a distilled water (aqua). And set a little aside for distilling, this water helps against coughing and against malignant diseases when drunk. When drunk on an empty stomach, warm, in the morning, it is good; if colder, after supper it makes one sleep well and rest well; taken with castoreum, warm, it is good for epilepsy and helps paralyzed limbs, and for the sluggish it stirs the humors, and strengthens weak heads, and gives great benefit.

Water of the Hen (Aqua Galine)

Sage water, decocted with sage and pennyroyal, prepared together in a mortar.

Set this aside for distilling; this water, drunk warm, warms a cold womb when cooked with castoreum. Drink it frequently on an empty stomach; it strengthens a cold heart and purges all poison, and helps hearing in all malignancies, except for gout. It is good for the complexion and gives one a good color; it restores the face and makes it fair. Taken warm three times a day, it is good against swellings and pains of the womb, and washed it heals as well.

Note that as much of this water as is needed should be used in preparing the distillation, with the water of Alban added, with proportions and doses as prescribed with castoreum and rhubarb and sugar, cooked for a long time until it is sufficiently reduced, and this medicine is good for all the maladies of the body mentioned, whoever takes it and uses it in the proper measure and manner, as prescribed, will recover. And if any other morbid infirmity has befallen, with the aforesaid waters, the water of Alban should be applied in due proportion, and as prescribed, boiled as above, and let it wash the infirmity.

translation: ...from corrupted and excessive humors which cause pain. These must be cured and the body cleansed of such humors. If the patient perceives much frost, chill, and cold, and seems to stand upon ice, the physician must act, for this illness is cold [in nature], hardened and in need of warming. If the sick person perceives, as it were, pomp, flames, fire, and lightning flashing, along with distress and conflict and all manner of disturbance, the physician must treat this illness and its excessive heat, which requires cure and cooling, as against cold. If the patient perceives himself as if drowning and struggling and swimming and feeling himself wallowing, the physician must treat the weakened state of the patient, with care and with the memory of all that is pleasant, and with joyful matters, delightful and sweet drink; and if he perceives conflict, such that the blood flows and he sees a red color, the physician must treat the patient and apply the appropriate remedy—vomiting, cupping, and bloodletting; and if bleeding is excessive, it must be reduced and expelled. If the sick person perceives various colors shifting, and all such things that pertain to migraine, the physician must treat the patient accordingly with suitable medicine. If the patient feels himself approaching danger, near to weakness, with difficulty and distress, the physician must treat the patient for corrupted humors and foul condition. If the sick person perceives pomp, as though he were being burned and suffering greatly, and feels as if suffocating, the physician must act according to the art and skill required. If the illness has progressed along its course and reached the vital passages, and the sick person perceives various images presented to him, the physician must treat accordingly with careful consideration and study. Here I begin to set forth
this aforementioned book, which I
must name according to necessity.
I will arrange this little book
in an order, so that one
can more easily recognize
what is written in this book,

book into four parts.

remedies are not known in all lands;
some are known here, some elsewhere.

many names, many languages,

Betony grows in rocky places,
as well on arable land and on meadows,
and on mountains and in common
places. In young growth it has 76
virtues, as will hereafter be explained.

That a person may have a healthy constitution and
steady, clear eyes and a fresh
head, one should always keep Betony
in a cup or in a glass
and drink from it: early and
late, when needed, either on an empty stomach or
with food. It should also lie day and
night in the wine. One should also
measure it properly, but give it fresh each day, and
it is good that the person remain cheerful

and that melancholy and sadness not
oppress him, and that he be of good cheer. One should
take Betony and old wine and
myrrh and boil them well
together, and one should drink from it for three
days. This is good, so that the person gains a good
complexion and color, even if he weeps.

translation:
Whoever finds himself weakened by illness should take two drachms of betony and warm water, two parts, and mix them well together, and drink it; that helps. When a person feels weak and faint and cannot go about well, one should take betony and the roots and grind them to powder, and let him take them by mouth; that makes a person strong and vigorous again. For the weakness before illness, this remedy may keep him so that he does not sink from exhaustion.

For excessive weakness, one should take two drachms of betony and two parts of mulsa (honeyed wine), and drink it; it quickly does good and helps one who vomits blood from the mouth or has some other ailment, or who vomits forcefully, so that he may be helped by it.

One should also drink chekonita mixed equally with pufcha — pufcha being made of two parts water and one third [something else] — for one whose throat hurts and who is unwell. One should boil betony in strong wine and drink from it, and apply the herb warm around the throat and bind it; this makes a person healthy again.

When the affliction causes pain, or moistness, or weakness so that one cannot keep down food, one should take a drachm and a half (that is, two guldens' worth) and mix it with two parts of warm water, and drink it; that helps.

translation:
To bring up what causes the chest to hurt, or
discomfort: For one whose chest hurts,
one should take betony with honey,
and this is good for many ailments and
illnesses of the chest, and it helps against
congestion around the chest. One should
take betony mixed well with mulsa (honey-wine),
and crush it, and drink it; this same
remedy clears obstruction and drives out
all impurity from the chest. Mulsa
is made thus: one takes one part
water and calls it one part honey,
and mixes it through another, that is
mulsa. For one who has a sick stomach,
one should take a drachm and
eat it with vinegar for three days, and in between
with water, and this should be drunk
on top; this helps the stomach and
strengthens it. For one whose liver is
unhealthy, one should take a drachm
of betony, and for three days
place it in warm water,
and from this one should drink. For one
whose bladder hurts, one should take
betony, a drachm, and three
parts of the root, and this should be boiled
down by half, and then this
should be drunk; this helps eternally and
always. For one whose back or sides
or ribs hurt, one should
also take what is written next.

translation: Betony and pepper taken with warm wine, drunk fasting, is good. For one whose teeth continually ache—that is, when it is pressing or sore inside—one should boil betony well in wine and drink that. For one whose teeth ache and are loose, one should take a dram of betony and also pepper-corns, and these should be ground together and drunk in warm wine, fasting, as a good remedy. For aching thighs or teeth, or for looseness, one should take a dram of betony and drink that with mulsa (honeyed wine). The mixture consists of one part water and a ninth part honey, blended together. For pain in the joints, one should take a dram of betony, mix it in due measure with warm wine, and drink from that. For pain in the hips, one should take a dram of betony and sixteen pepper-corns, and these should be crushed and, in due measure, taken with warm wine while fasting—this cleanses the hip joint. For one whose hip-joint is sore, one should take a dram of betony with pepper-corns, crush them, and take with wine while fasting. For pain that settles in the blade-bone (shoulder blade), one should take a dram of betony with vinegar and an ounce of honey.

translation:
One shall take two drams of betony and
nine measures of hydromel, and these shall be
mixed, and drunk from this, which opens
the bowels. Also, that which is called hydromel
is made by taking two parts of water and
one third part of honey, and mixing it, heating it
together, and of this one shall take nine measures.

For one who may [suffer with] the stool or with cramps or
convulsions, one shall take betony
powder and with honey near a slow-cooking
heat let it blend thoroughly together, and
take the same every day — this helps.
For one who may [suffer] a burst [hernia/rupture], one
shall take betony with good wine to
drink, which makes the person's
flow of water [urine] pass better. For one whose water
cannot be voided properly, one shall drink betony,
two drams, which also drives out the stone
from the bladder. When a person has eaten
poison, one shall take betony, two
drams, and two measures of wine, and this
drink at once, which casts the poison back
out and restores the person
fresh and healthy again. For one who has had enough
of poison and needs no more [to expel],
one shall take betony mixed well with wine,
which drives the poison back out, whether one
has such about or not; one should take the herb,
which is fresh and wholesome. For one afflicted
with dropsy (water sickness), one shall
drink betony with water or with wine.

also has the virtue that a person always

Celandine juice and fennel juice mixed with fresh woman's milk, and with this anoint the eyes. Whoever has any small blemish in the eyes: one should press celandine through a clean cloth and lay this same juice upon the blemish. Whoever's eyes are dark on account of the veins, for this one should mix celandine juice equally with old wine and anoint the eyes with it - that heals them well and helps.

Whoever has pain in the teeth should crush celandine roots and hold them in the mouth - this takes away the pain from the teeth. Whoever has a blemish/mole on the body or on the face: one should make celandine leaves into powder and crush them with wine - this same should drive away the blemish wherever one applies it, and it also helps well and is proven. Whoever is unwell within the body should make celandine root into powder and mix it with anise, and warm this together in good wine - this helps and is well proven.

Rue is called wine-rue and has manifold virtues. Whoever has headache should crush rue juice with rose oil and mix it well with vinegar, and with this anoint the head - that is healthy [helps]. Whoever's head has broken out with impurity [i.e. sores/scabs]...

One should mix cabbage juice with fennel juice
and pure honey in equal measure, as much of one
as of the other, and also mix them well together,
and so put this mixture into the eyes without
hesitation; this clears away the cloudiness in the eyes
and makes the eyes bright
and clear. When the eyes are swollen or
inflamed, one should drink broth with cabbage juice;
this takes away the redness from
the eyes and restores health. For one whose
eyes hurt and are
swollen, one should mix cabbage juice
with rose oil and vinegar and
white lead in equal parts, and
this should be poured into the nose,
there where it smells strongly and causes watering.

For one whose nose tends to bleed too much,
one should pour cabbage juice into
the nose; this stops the bleeding.
When speech is lost or impaired
due to some obstruction, one should give cabbage
juice mixed with vinegar to drink immediately,
until he speaks again, when the throat
has been affected badly. One should
let him drink this cabbage mixture often; this is
certainly good for that. For one who
wishes to prepare a drink for another,
one should pound cabbage into powder.

And boil all the wounds together with blood in wine and drink of it every night; for one who is wounded or beaten and wishes to be healed, one should make rue stirred with egg, and this should be laid at once upon the wounds; this heals. For whom the [wound] is made inflamed and festering, one should pound rue well with laurel leaves and lay this upon the inflamed wound; this helps.

For whom the self (body) becomes impure, one should drink rue before the person urinates.

For which woman something is wrong with her womb, or who is not healthy [there], one should [prepare] rue with butter and with little else, all together; this should be made warm, and it helps the womb when it is disordered, and it helps one whose belly does not hold [food], and it helps against all the ailments that are within the person, and it makes the person healthy.

For which woman has trouble in her private parts, one should drink rue often; this cleanses her also in her private parts and her affliction.

For which woman labors or is in [the process of] fruit [childbirth], one should drink rue often, or in the wine in which it has been placed; this helps her.

For one who has a sore on the head:
one should take betony, crush it with oil or by hand,
and with it anoint the sore; upon
the head it will be healing, truly. For one whose
eyes are swollen, one should take green roots of
violet, measure them, and good saffron,
crush them together, and with this
one should anoint the eyes well at night.

For one whose nose smells foul, one should
take betony with [an herb], crush it well, and
put it into the nose; this drives away the stench.

For one who cannot speak, one should
take betony, crush it with wine, and give it to drink;
this will make the person speak again,
and must [be given]. For one who has a sick stomach:
one should boil betony in water and
drink from it; this helps the stomach and its
[complaints], when the stomach does not ache. One
should boil betony-roots with vinegar and
drink this off; it helps and drives out the weakness
and melancholy that comes from it. For one
whose humor is disordered, one should take
betony-roots, set them with vinegar, and give this to drink;
it helps the stomach for one whose heart is troubled.
One should prepare betony this way; it makes the
belly soft and relieves it. For one whose excess
blood in the body is too strong, one should take
likewise green or [dried] plums, boil them in water, and
drink this off while warm; and for worms as well.

one should crush violet leaves with chicken fat and with
vinegar, pound them together, and apply them; that is called old
wounds. For whoever has a wound that will not close,
one should wash violets and apply them in the mouth.

translation:
Whoever wants to make hair grow all over

One should take hair oil and set it aside. From the top of the hair strands one should take a portion, and should take five or six portions of olive oil, and apply the hair oil to it in a glass, placed on top, and should seal the glass well on both ends, and let it flow together into itself and let it stand for six days, undisturbed, and the hair oil should be [applied] all around. It is good for many purposes, such as making unsightly skin smooth and sleek.

For one whose head aches:

One should anoint the head with hair oil as prescribed, or one should drink hair oil—that is good for the head and helps.

For one whose throat aches:

One should keep hair oil running in the mouth; that helps well.

For one whose stomach aches:

One should boil water thoroughly in water and drink it when it has cooled, or one may drink it with milk; that helps the stomach's excess heat and makes one cheerful.

For one who has flux in the belly:

One should drink hair oil, or give others a drink of it, which warms the belly and drives away excess heat from the stomach.

For one who wishes to heal wounds, or wherever one is badly wounded:

One should anoint the wounds with hair oil as prescribed; this heals them from the root, and it also greatly helps against infection from the wound.

translation:
Centaury, or fever-herb, is of two kinds: one is gray and the other blue, though the blue kind is more common, and here we shall speak of this one, as it has several virtues. For one whose head aches: one should mix centaury juice with vinegar, warm it, and anoint the head with it while warm. For one whose eyes ache: one should boil centaury with honey and wash the eyes with it; this makes the eyes clear and sharpens the sight against dullness. For one who has no appetite for food and suffers from indigestion: one should boil centaury in water, and drink it warm for three days; this makes the person have an appetite again and helps him to feel refreshed.

If a person has eaten or drunk something harmful, one should make a powder of centaury, and of this powder take two quintins (a small weight), boiled and drunk in wine; this helps and refreshes what the person has taken in. Or, one may mix centaury with vinegar and drink it; it will quickly expel whatever is harmful within the body.

For one who wishes to help the stomach, chest, and cough: one should take centaury, salt, and wine, and a third part water, and mix this with honey, boiling and straining it well; this mixture helps the stomach and clears the chest.

For one who suffers great thirst from fever: one should boil centaury in water and drink it cold; this helps as well.

If the eyes ache, one should take the juice of [the herb] and put a little of it in a vial, let it steep, and then put it on the eyes at night like a plaster. For one who has freckles or wants to remove spots, one should take [the herb] with [another substance] in a vial, and mix it with the juice and put it on the spots or freckles, so that they fade away and the skin becomes clear. translation:
One should seek this [remedy] among men and drink it down,
and this helps against all thirst, whether one is eating or
drinking, whatever was received or is present.

For one who desires to eat or drink,
one should seek this among men and drink it down;
this helps the one who wants to eat but has no appetite
either to eat or to drink; or one should
lay this plaster upon the breast, so the
person will be eager to eat again.

For one whose thirst troubles him:
one should seek this in water and drink it down;
this helps against the thirst, and
for one whose stomach is always hungry and yet not
healthy.

For one whose fat (or skin) troubles him, one should
seek this fat among men and drink it;
this helps one whose flank hurts, for one
whose fat in the skull aches so badly that
blood comes forth from the person. One should
seek this in water and drink it
down; this makes the person better. For one who has worms
in the ears: one should seek this fat, this plaster,
and let it drip warm into the ear; this
kills the worms in the ear and takes away
the pain. For one through whom blood flows, one
should lay this fat mixed with food as a plaster
and apply another one upon the breast, and also
drink this down; this stops the blood. On another
matter concerning this fat: all these things should
be made into food with fat, and eaten and drunk; this
preserves them in a good condition and with their proper strength.

Lettuce is a good herb and it is useful
whenever the eyes are dry.
One should crush lettuce leaves and
mix them with honey bread, and with that
one should anoint the eyes; this is a particularly
good remedy, in particular that derived from lettuce.
One reads that when the eagle wishes to fly very high,
it is because of lettuce that makes its
sight so sharp and clear, that it has many
secret properties, high and fine.
This same property comes from lettuce. For whoever has
eye pain, one should give lettuce
juice to eat and drink, gently, which
greatly helps the stomach and its causes, and the
eyes, and makes them bright and clear.
If a woman has little milk and has a child,
she should often take lettuce juice, which increases the
woman's milk, which also nourishes children, and
helps the stomach to be at peace and
removes excess heat. If a person's
body is unsettled, one should take lettuce seed with wine
to drink; this settles the body's disturbance
and brings the person inner calm.
For a special remedy made from lettuce for the eyes:
One should take lettuce and old wine and
goat's gall and mix them all together
with another substance, and apply it to the eyes with
a clean application, and for darkness
in the eyes, this thereafter should be
applied, and it makes an excellent remedy. 24

put it in a cloth, and lay it on the spot

And if there is no sap in it, then one shall
plaster it with the same and lay it on the wound,
or wherever a person has been struck hard,
that heals by the hand within that same day
once it is applied or pressed on. Then one
shall remove it again, for it is a strange
remedy, and it will have worked within that same day.

Whoever wants to remove freckles or blemishes,
one should make a plaster of celandine herb with honey,
and with it one shall
treat the blemishes or spots;
this removes the spots and makes the person's
skin tender and clear. Wherever it is on
the body, if blood flows through the person,
one should plaster celandine and press out
the juice; that helps the person through it,
making the blood good. Whoever vomits blood
from the mouth, one should make a plaster of celandine herb
and press it on; that helps the one who
vomits blood. For one whose ears hurt,
one should mix celandine juice with warm melissa (balm),
and prepare it to be liquid and smooth, and
pour it warm into the ears. So that a person
who is weakened by sickness may recover strength,
one should eat celandine prepared in this way; that helps
so that the person is not made ill in that regard.
Concerning especially burning sensations from celandine, one
shall take celandine juice, two parts, and
one third part honey, and mix them together.

For this remedy one shall use all manner of healing herbs and mix them together, or apply a poultice that draws out matter. Whoever wishes to help with a swelling underneath: one shall press garlic together with tame fat (lard) and lay it upon the place of the swelling, that drives away the swelling on a person, an especially good remedy.

Onion has many virtues; whoever wishes to guard himself against bad air should [use it well].

translation:
Handtritt (plantain, "hand-step") is a good herb by its very name.

For whoever suffers from a wound caused by treading, one should pound the handtritt herb and apply it together with its juice to the swollen sores, or onto the affected part or spot; this will heal it completely. Whoever wishes to have black hair should pound handtritt well together with oil and crush it thoroughly, then frequently rub the hair with it — this will turn the hair black.

Wegwart (chicory) is a good herb for whoever wants help against poison.

One should drink the juice of wegwart, or one should drink the powdered herb mixed with wine, or one should drink wine in which wegwart has been boiled. This helps against all poison; whoever makes regular use of it, it keeps the body steady and healthy.

Ulstritt is a good herb for one whose throat pains them somewhat. One should pound the leaves of ulstritt and drink the juice, or make it into powder, or use the water in which ulstritt has been boiled. When one goes hunting, or one should wind ulstritt into a wreath/band and bind it around the neck, and that shall prove very good.

Nerstrichung is a good, noble herb that is good for the milk; one should take it to heart.

translation:
This helps for the wound that has become inflamed: whoever wishes to make the wound tame and heal should take the leaves of nettleburr (?) and pound them, and with the juice lay it upon the wound; this will draw off the corruption from the wound caused by bad matter and bad pus. Whoever wishes help against poison that has entered the body should drink nettleburr mixed with [something]; this helps against poison of the nose.

Schwartz (black root) is of two kinds: one grows in water, the other kind grows in the garden. If one wishes to [use it], one should let the black root become dry and then grind it well; the powder should be ground together, two parts of one thing to a little of another, with water — this helps for the swelling when the testicle aches. One should mix the black root well with [another substance], driving it through one another, and this mixture should be heated and then applied, taken off again when warm. For this is also useful for [wounds] that have gone bad, one should take the little black root and give it to drink in [wine/water].

The sword-lily (Schwertel/Iris) is likewise another kind of root; it has yellow leaves, like the blue-leaved kind, and its leaves grow up out of the earth; one often finds it in gardens. It helps with burns from sparks; one should boil the short sword-lily root in water and then let it dry. Whoever wishes to keep bees in a hive should put the sword-lily root among the bees; this way the bees will not be harmed [or similar].

translation:
Wound

This makes the wound firm so that it does not grow worse.
And that the stones [swellings?] on the sick person be opened up [treated by application].
Without pain, one shall have the heart [herb] well boiled,
and afterward lay it upon the wound.
With this one shall also anoint the sick person's gums [pillars/jaws] with the same.
When the wounds hurt and grow worse,
one shall moisten what is affected, boiled well with vinegar,
and afterward lay it upon the wound.
This makes the wound fresh and healthy.
Or one shall take good camphor mixed with fibers [lint]
into the wounds, and this one shall mix with hay [or similar].
Or one shall take pepper and boil it with the stones,
and keep it warm in the mouth.
Or, as stated on the first day it is written, concerning
the "pleytetten" and about "vbena" and about "mincher,"
and about "betfanica," one shall boil fine leather
in water well, and with this one shall
wash the mouth well. Or one shall boil sugar in
wine well, and lay that upon the wound and upon
the gums. Or one shall boil violets and
hold that in the mouth. Or one shall take wormwood
and hellebore with vinegar, the wounds
warm, and lay that upon the wound to keep.
Or one shall boil borage root well in wine,
and with this one shall wash the mouth. All
remedies for the wall [gums?], or one shall let fall the
yellow stone [substance], and that one anoint the wounds with it.

translation:
On how one who wishes to treat a cut wound of the neck should proceed. One
should keep the neck protected in this way, [to protect] against bad wounds
from foul air, which is good for many kinds of causes
that arise from it, by which people develop
swelling at the neck and from which people get
roughness, and from which comes the sprouting of mucus
in the throat and, from within the body, sickness,
a strange misfortune of the neck, from swelling of the throat,
from which they get a choking desire and fall down and die.
One should note that the mischief comes down
into the throat so that the person cannot breathe and may see
that the swelling travels into the throat and
rises up at the back of the throat and firmly
closes, as it were, a bolt that is there in the throat,
the other part goes outward through the same opening,
and when the throat is thus swollen inside, the person
can draw no breath and must suffocate.
And it spreads as quickly as if one did something to the feet;
therefore one should take care of it promptly, so that everything
may be relieved as soon as possible, and that one
should turn to it carefully and then apply a good plaster,
and one should see to it that the swollen area is well drained,
and that the matter grows thick like foam,
and this one should, while still warm, apply around the neck,
and on both sides one should let blood from the veins beneath [it].

In this way, death shall not befall him from it.
[Here] the other part of this chapter on healing is the
poultice, as written above, and this further...
